templates.name: Blank completion, phrase options (word + preposition, a/an + word)
Most nearly mean, underlined phrase or phrase options
Blank completion, cause or consequence clue
Blank completion, contrast clue (including received view then finding)

items.passage: Crown-of-thorns seastars, notorious coral predators, are herbivorous as juveniles, feeding on algae. In experiments by Dione Deaker and colleagues, juveniles maintained on algae for six and a half years reached a diameter of about 16 to 18 millimeters and then stopped growing, remaining that size for years until they were finally offered coral; in this species, then, size can be largely ______ age.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be decoupled from something is to be separated from it, so that the two no longer change together. Juveniles kept on algae “stopped growing” at about 16 to 18 millimeters, “remaining that size for years,” so a seastar of that size could be young or several years old: its size can be largely separated from its age.

A.why_wrong: Inextricable from means impossible to separate from. The text shows the opposite: juveniles stopped growing and kept the same size “for years,” so their size came apart from their age.

B.why_wrong: Emblematic of means serving as a symbol of. Nothing in the text treats a seastar’s size as a symbol of its age; the point is that size and age can come apart.

D.why_wrong: Antecedent to means coming before. The text says nothing about size coming before age; it shows that size stopped changing while the seastars kept getting older.

band7_moves: consequence is the only clue (size stays fixed for years, so it stops tracking age)

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Deaker et al. 2020 (Biology Letters): crown-of-thorns juveniles are herbivorous before switching to coral; cohorts reared on crustose coralline algae for 10 months and 6.5 years both reached an asymptotic size of 16-18 mm on algae; after 6.5 years of herbivory they were competent coral predators; 'a marked age-size disconnect'

items.notes: Subject: natural science (marine ecology). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (size fixed for years while the animals age, so size no longer tracks age). Concessive frame: no. Transferred-sense key: no. Raw freq.txt ranks: inextricable from 34,178; emblematic of 28,969; decoupled from unseen (1,000,000); antecedent to 35,359 (4 of 4 past 10,000, 4 past 20,000). Band-5 guard: clear (all distractors rare). Recipes ANT + 2 UNSUP, as in band-7 a06c434d. The source says 'age-size disconnect'; the key is a different word and the passage uses neither.

band7.why: Recounted from freq.txt: inextricable from 34,178, emblematic of 28,969, antecedent to 35,359, decoupled from unseen (4 of 4 past 10,000). The key's unseen rank is partly a corpus artifact (pre-1928 Gutenberg; 1 hit in the modern federal texts, under the 3-hit correction, and it occurs in CB's own R&W text), so the three distractors at 29k to 35k carry the set. Two steps (size fixed for years while the animals age, so size stops tracking age); the passage never restates the key with a familiar word. Combined gate passes, band-5 guard clear.

items.passage: As common noctule bats have colonized hibernation sites at increasingly northern latitudes, young males appear to have constituted the ______ of that expansion. In a recently colonized hibernation area studied by Kseniia Kravchenko and colleagues, first-year males were especially abundant during the early stages of colonization, and the population’s age and sex composition became more balanced only gradually.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A vanguard is the group at the front of a movement, the first to arrive. In the newly colonized area, “first-year males were especially abundant during the early stages of colonization,” and the population’s makeup “became more balanced only gradually,” so young males led the way north.

B.why_wrong: Progeny means offspring. First-year males are the offspring of older bats, but the blank names the part they played in the move north, and the text stresses that they arrived first, not whose young they were.

C.why_wrong: A bulwark is a defensive wall or a strong protection. Nothing in the text says that young males defended or protected anything; it says only that they were abundant early in the colonization.

D.why_wrong: The rearguard is the group at the back of a moving force. The text says the reverse: first-year males were abundant in “the early stages of colonization,” and the mix of bats became more balanced “only gradually.”

band7_moves: familiar word in a transferred sense (military vanguard for the first animals to colonize)
clue in a plainer register than the key (abundant in the early years)
all four options past rank 10,000, three past 20,000

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Kravchenko et al. 2020 (Biology Letters), 'first-year males lead the way to hibernacula at higher latitudes': colonization of hibernation sites further north; in a recently colonized hibernation area, subadult males were more abundant during the early colonization stage, followed by a gradual shift to a more balanced age and sex composition

items.notes: Subject: natural science (mammal ecology). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (first-year males abundant first, others later, so they were the leading group; then the transferred military word). Concessive frame: no. Transferred-sense key: yes. Raw freq.txt ranks: vanguard 28,066; progeny 31,731; bulwark 18,088; rearguard 40,681 (4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000). Band-5 guard: clear. Harbinger was left out because it would be a second defensible answer.

band7.why: Recounted: vanguard 28,066, progeny 31,731, bulwark 18,088, rearguard 40,681 (4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000). Familiar military word in a transferred sense, clue in a plainer register (abundant in the early stages); progeny is a live topic-echo trap for 'first-year males'. Rearguard is a plain reversal, the commonest band-7 recipe after UNSUP. No familiar key restated by the passage.

items.passage: Cleaner shrimp remove parasites and dead skin from fish, including species that could easily devour them. Eleanor Caves and colleagues found that the cleaner shrimp Lysmata amboinensis is decidedly ______ with such risky clients: it cleaned predatory fish in a smaller proportion of interactions than nonpredatory fish, and it performed a leg-rocking display, possibly signaling an intent to clean, almost exclusively toward predators.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Circumspect means careful and wary of risk. The shrimp “cleaned predatory fish in a smaller proportion of interactions than nonpredatory fish” and directed its leg-rocking display “almost exclusively toward predators,” so it treats the clients that could devour it with particular care.

A.why_wrong: Intrepid means fearless. A fearless shrimp would have no reason to clean predators less often, yet this shrimp cleaned them “in a smaller proportion of interactions than nonpredatory fish.”

B.why_wrong: Obstreperous means noisy and unruly. The text describes a shrimp that holds back with dangerous clients and signals before cleaning, not one that behaves wildly.

C.why_wrong: Indolent means lazy. The shrimp did clean predators less often, but only predators, and it added a display directed at them, so the change answers to the danger those clients pose rather than showing a lack of effort.

band7_moves: partly right distractor built from half the evidence (indolent: cleans less, but only predators)
all four options past rank 10,000, three past 20,000

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Caves, Chen and Johnsen 2019 (Biology Letters): cleaner shrimp remove ectoparasites and dead skin from clients, many of which are potential predators; Lysmata amboinensis cleaned predatory clients in a significantly lower proportion of interactions and showed leg rocking, potentially signalling identity or intent to clean, almost exclusively toward predatory clients

items.notes: Subject: natural science (marine behavior). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (fewer cleanings and a special display only toward predators, so the shrimp is managing a risk; then the rare word for wary care). Concessive frame: no. Transferred-sense key: no. Raw freq.txt ranks: intrepid 23,449; obstreperous 39,175; indolent 10,362; circumspect 27,384 (4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000). Band-5 guard: clear. Obsequious was left out (the display could be read as eager to please).

band7.why: Recounted: intrepid 23,449, obstreperous 39,175, indolent 10,362, circumspect 27,384 (4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000). Indolent is a partly right near miss built from half the evidence (cleans predators less often); the key needs the second half (a display aimed at predators). No familiar key restated.

items.passage: Most large raptors avoid crossing the sea during migration, since temperate seas generate little of the atmospheric convection, or rising warm air, on which soaring birds depend. But juvenile ospreys tracked by Olivier Duriez and colleagues located and exploited thermals about 7.5 times per 100 kilometers over the Mediterranean, suggesting that open water may be a less ______ barrier to large raptors than is widely assumed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Insuperable means impossible to overcome. Large raptors usually avoid the sea, but the tracked ospreys “located and exploited thermals” over the Mediterranean, so open water may be easier to overcome than “is widely assumed”: less insuperable.

A.why_wrong: Navigable means able to be traveled across. The ospreys’ use of thermals over the sea suggests open water is more crossable than assumed, so calling it less navigable reverses the finding.

C.why_wrong: Expansive means covering a wide area. The finding concerns whether raptors can cross the sea, not its size; finding thermals over the water does not make the sea any smaller.

D.why_wrong: Inconspicuous means hard to notice. The text says nothing about how noticeable the sea is to migrating birds; a less inconspicuous barrier would be a more noticeable one, which has nothing to do with the ospreys’ use of thermals.

band7_moves: negation hidden in a comparative (a less ______ barrier than is widely assumed)

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Duriez et al. 2018 (Biology Letters): most large raptors avoid crossing the sea because of the lack of atmospheric convection over temperate seas; five GPS-tracked juvenile ospreys found and used thermal uplift while crossing the Mediterranean, on average 7.5 times per 100 km; results question the widely held assumption that water bodies are strict barriers for large raptors

items.notes: Subject: natural science (bird migration). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (raptors avoid the sea, ospreys still find lift there, so the barrier is weaker than believed; then undo 'less ... than assumed'). Concessive frame: no (contrast with 'But'). Transferred-sense key: no. Raw freq.txt ranks: navigable 39,164; insuperable 24,338; expansive 21,169; inconspicuous 31,644 (4 of 4 past 20,000). Band-5 guard: clear. Formidable, impassable, perilous and inhospitable were left out: each would also fit 'less ______ than assumed'.

band7.why: Recounted: navigable 39,164, insuperable 24,338, expansive 21,169, inconspicuous 31,644 (4 of 4 past 20,000). Negation hidden in a comparative ('a less ______ barrier ... than is widely assumed'), with navigable as the reversal a student picks if the comparative is not undone. No familiar key restated.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Thomas Hardy’s 1887 novel The Woodlanders. Mr. Melbury, a timber merchant in a small English village, is talking with Giles, a family friend, about his daughter, Grace, who is about to come home after being away at a fashionable school.

“[N]aturally we shall look small, just at first—I only say just at first.”

Mr. Melbury’s tone evinced a certain exultation in the very sense of that inferiority he <u>affected</u> to deplore; for this advanced and refined being, was she not his own all the time?
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “affected” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: In this context, “affected” means pretended. Melbury says the family will “look small” beside Grace, as if he regrets it, yet his “tone evinced a certain exultation” in that very inferiority, because Grace, so “advanced and refined,” is his own daughter. His regret is only for show.

B.why_wrong: “Affected” can mean influenced, as when rain affects a harvest, but that sense does not fit “affected to deplore,” and it misses the contrast between the regret Melbury expresses and the pride his tone shows.

C.why_wrong: “Affected” can mean emotionally touched, but that would make Melbury’s regret sincere, whereas the text says his tone showed “a certain exultation” in the inferiority he spoke of.

D.why_wrong: “Affected” can mean concerned or involved, as when a storm affects several towns, but that sense does not describe how Melbury speaks about the family’s inferiority.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of The Woodlanders (Thomas Hardy, 1887): Melbury blacks the horse's hoofs before Grace's return; 'naturally we shall look small, just at first' and the narrator's comment, copied exactly (capital N bracketed)

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1887). Key letter A. Band 6 per WAVE.md (M1 hard written as a strong band 6, like 9b22bf7b determine/Dictate). The trap is the sincere sense (Touched); the clue that defeats it is 'exultation'. Excerpt trimmed at the start of the quoted speech ('[N]aturally'), otherwise exact. Hardy's The Woodlanders appears in no official item and none of ours (The Mayor of Casterbridge is a round-1 draft); 'affected' rank 3,415 for the key Pretended.

band7.why: Template written to a strong band 6 by plan. The target (affected, 2,434) and key (Pretended, 3,415) are common words; the item rests on the secondary sense against the sincere-sense trap (Touched), defeated by 'exultation'. Strong band 6, not band 7.

items.passage: From the 1950s onward, Brazilian artist Rubem Valentim produced paintings that were thoroughly ______: in them, emblems of the orishas (deities) worshipped in Candomblé, an Afro-Brazilian religion, such as Shango’s double-bladed axe and Oshosi’s arrow, are rendered in the vocabulary of geometric abstraction, an artistic idiom that originated in Europe and that Valentim adopted in those same years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Syncretic means combining different traditions or systems of belief. Valentim’s paintings render “emblems of the orishas” of Candomblé, an Afro-Brazilian religion, “in the vocabulary of geometric abstraction,” an idiom “that originated in Europe,” so each painting joins the two traditions.

A.why_wrong: Parochial means narrowly local. The Candomblé emblems come from Afro-Brazilian culture, but the paintings render them in an idiom “that originated in Europe,” so the work is not narrowly local.

B.why_wrong: Iconoclastic means attacking cherished beliefs or sacred images. Valentim’s paintings take up the sacred emblems of Candomblé rather than attacking them.

C.why_wrong: Derivative means imitating others’ work without originality. Valentim did use a European idiom, but he used it to render Afro-Brazilian emblems, joining two traditions rather than copying one.

band7_moves: examples instantiate an abstract category (two traditions joined in one painting)
half-clue distractors, one for each tradition (parochial, derivative)

sources.what: e-flux announcement of MASP's Rubem Valentim: Afro-Atlantic Constructions (2018-2019): from the 1950s Valentim used the language of geometric abstraction, an idiom of European origin, with emblems of the orishas such as Shango's double-bladed axe and Oshosi's arrow; by 1955 he resolved to work with references from Candomble and Afro-Brazilian culture

items.notes: Subject: humanities (Brazilian art). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (identify the two traditions in the examples, then name their combination). Concessive frame: no. Transferred-sense key: yes, mild (syncretic is usually said of religions). Raw freq.txt ranks: parochial 22,657; iconoclastic 51,496; derivative 31,569; syncretic unseen (1,000,000) (4 of 4 past 20,000; rarest distractor past 50,000). Band-5 guard: clear. Eclectic and hybrid were left out (either could be defended).

band7.why: Recounted: parochial 22,657, iconoclastic 51,496, derivative 31,569 raw (lower once modern usage is credited), syncretic unseen (3 of 4 past 10,000 on either measure; rarest distractor past 50,000). Example-pinned abstract category with two half-clue distractors (parochial, derivative), one per tradition. No familiar key restated.

items.passage: Kaitlin Woolley and Ayelet Fishbach found that strangers who had eaten from a single shared plate were less ______ during negotiations than were strangers who had eaten identical food from separate plates, apparently because sharing a plate increased the diners’ perception that they had been coordinating their behavior.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Combative means eager to fight or argue. Sharing a plate “increased the diners’ perception that they had been coordinating their behavior,” so during negotiations they were less inclined to fight with the other side than were strangers who had eaten from separate plates.

A.why_wrong: Accommodating means willing to help or give way. Diners who felt they “had been coordinating their behavior” would be more accommodating, not less, so this choice reverses the finding.

C.why_wrong: Talkative means inclined to talk a lot. The text says nothing about how much the diners spoke; it is about how they treated one another during negotiations.

D.why_wrong: Ravenous means extremely hungry. The text is about eating, but the blank describes how diners behaved during negotiations, and nothing suggests that sharing a plate changed their hunger.

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Woolley and Fishbach 2019 (Psychological Science), 'Shared Plates, Shared Minds': people eating from shared plates cooperated more in social dilemmas and negotiations than those eating from separate plates; sharing a plate increased perceived coordination, which led diners to behave more cooperatively and less competitively; the effect occurred among strangers

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology). Key letter B. Negated frame 'less ______ ... than'. Raw freq.txt ranks: accommodating 13,738; combative 30,128; talkative 13,443; ravenous 16,949 (medium band). Recipes: negation flip, UNSUP, topic echo (eating).

items.passage: English speakers may “see red” or “feel blue,” but are such associations between colors and emotions acquired through language and cultural tradition, or are they ______ human cognition? Surveying 4,598 participants from 30 nations, Domicele Jonauskaite and colleagues found that color-emotion associations were remarkably consistent internationally, although nations that were geographically or linguistically proximate exhibited especially similar patterns.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Fundamental to means forming a basic part of. The question sets this possibility against associations “acquired through language and cultural tradition,” and the finding that associations were “remarkably consistent internationally” points to links that belong to human cognition itself rather than to any one culture.

A.why_wrong: Incidental to means only a minor side effect of. The text contrasts learned associations with associations rooted in “human cognition,” and associations “remarkably consistent internationally” suggest something basic, not something minor.

B.why_wrong: Detrimental to means harmful to. Nothing in the text suggests that links between colors and emotions harm human cognition.

D.why_wrong: Subordinate to means lower in rank than. The text does not rank color-emotion links below anything; it asks whether they are learned or part of cognition itself.

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Jonauskaite et al. 2020 (Psychological Science): asks whether color-emotion associations ('see red', 'feel blue') are fundamental to our shared cognitive architecture or cultural creations learned through languages and traditions; 4,598 participants from 30 nations; universal associations (average r = .88), greater similarity for linguistically or geographically close nations

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology of emotion). Key letter C. Contrast clue inside a question ('learned ... or ______'), confirmed by the finding. Raw freq.txt ranks: incidental to 19,860; detrimental to 28,955; fundamental to 15,122; subordinate to 13,590. The key matches the source's own framing; the passage does not use it.

items.passage: Hiri Motu, a simplified version of the Motu language of Papua New Guinea, derives its name from the hiri, the traditional trading expeditions of the Motu people. The language’s widespread distribution, however, is attributable in large part to the colonial constabulary, or police force, which so thoroughly ______ Hiri Motu that it eventually became known as Police Motu.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Embraced means took up readily. The text credits the colonial constabulary, or police force, with much of the language’s “widespread distribution” and says it “eventually became known as Police Motu,” which shows how fully the police took the language up as their own.

B.why_wrong: Outlawed means banned. A police force that banned the language would not have helped it spread, and the language would hardly have been named after that force.

C.why_wrong: Transcribed means wrote down. The text says nothing about the police writing the language down; it says the police spread it so widely that it was named after them.

D.why_wrong: Parodied means imitated in a mocking way. Nothing in the text suggests the police mocked the language; their role was to spread it.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Hiri Motu: a simplified version of Motu; hiri is the name of the traditional trade voyages of the Motu people; its use was spread through adoption by the Royal Papuan Constabulary, hence the name Police Motu

items.notes: Subject: social science (linguistics, with colonial history). Key letter A. Restatement clue: 'spread ... owed to the colonial police force' and 'came to be called Police Motu'. Raw freq.txt ranks: embraced 4,387; outlawed 11,129; transcribed 32,187; parodied 47,407. The key is the commonest option; the source word 'adoption' is not used.

items.passage:
The following text is from Rudyard Kipling’s 1897 novel Captains Courageous. Harvey, a teenager rescued at sea, is working aboard a fishing schooner off the coast of Newfoundland.

Next day they <u>fell in with</u> more sails [ships], all circling slowly from the east northerly towards the west. But just when they expected to make the shoals by the Virgin the fog shut down, and they anchored, surrounded by the tinklings of invisible bells. There was not much fishing, but occasionally dory [small boat] met dory in the fog and exchanged news.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “fell in with” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used in the text, “fell in with” means came across, or met. The schooner’s crew meets “more sails [ships], all circling slowly” toward the west, and the passage goes on to describe boats meeting at sea: “dory [small boat] met dory in the fog and exchanged news.”

A.why_wrong: To fall in with a plan can mean to agree with it, but the crew meets ships here; there is no plan or opinion to agree with.

B.why_wrong: To fall in with people can mean to become friendly with them, but the text describes the crew sighting other ships, not getting along with anyone.

C.why_wrong: The word “fell” might suggest a crash, but nothing in the text describes a collision; the ships are simply “circling slowly” nearby.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Captains Courageous (Rudyard Kipling, 1897), opening of chapter VII, copied exactly with two bracketed glosses

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1897). Key letter D. Phrase target with paraphrase options, as in 2.8 (reconcile his mother to). Nautical sense of 'fall in with' (to meet a ship). 'Joined' was left out (fall in = join ranks could be defended). Kipling appears in no official item and none of ours.

items.passage:
The following text is from Arnold Bennett’s 1910 novel Clayhanger. Edwin Clayhanger has just noticed the Vicar, a local clergyman, departing from the house that Edwin shares with his father and his sister, Maggie.

Maggie stood in the porch, which <u>commanded</u> the descent into Bursley; she was watching the Vicar as he receded. When Edwin appeared at the gate, she gave a little jump, and he fancied that she also blushed.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “commanded” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used in the text, “commanded” means faced, or looked out over. From the porch, Maggie is “watching the Vicar as he receded,” so the porch faces the descent, the downhill road, that he is walking along.

A.why_wrong: To command can mean to order, but a porch cannot give orders; the text uses the word for the view the porch offers.

C.why_wrong: To command can mean to earn or deserve, as in commanding respect, but the porch does not earn the descent; it faces it.

D.why_wrong: To command can mean to lead, as an officer commands troops, but nothing is being led here; Maggie is simply watching from the porch.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Clayhanger (Arnold Bennett, 1910): Edwin sees the elder Heve, vicar of Saint Peter's, coming away from the house; 'Maggie stood in the porch, which commanded the descent into Bursley', copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1910). Key letter B. Positional sense of 'command' (to face or look out over from above). Overlooked was avoided as the key (its common sense, failed to notice, would mislead), and Controlled was left out (a fort can command a pass in a military sense). Bennett's The Card and Anna of the Five Towns are ours; Clayhanger is unused anywhere.

items.passage: In the early paintings of his Écriture series, Korean painter Park Seo-bo repeatedly drew a pencil through a surface still wet with whitish paint, so that each pencil mark ______ some of the paint rather than adding anything to the surface. Park himself characterized this technique as a process of erasure.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Removed means took away. The text contrasts the blank with “adding anything to the surface” and says Park described his technique as “a process of erasure,” so each pencil mark took away some of the wet paint.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that the pencil marks protected the paint; Park called the technique “a process of erasure,” which means taking paint away.

B.why_wrong: The text does not say the pencil marks matched the paint in any way; it says they worked against adding anything to the surface.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text mentions the pencil marks making the paint brighter; the point is that each mark took paint away, as in erasure.

sources.what: Cleveland Museum of Art, Ecriture No. 22-77 (1977): Park repetitively incised the tip of the pencil into a surface still wet with whitish paint; the pencil mark removes paint; Park considers this a process of erasure. The passage limits the method to the series' early paintings (later works moved to hanji paper and other tools)

items.notes: Subject: humanities (Korean art). Key letter C. Restatement clue: 'rather than adding anything' and 'a process of erasure'. Raw freq.txt ranks: protected 2,995; matched 2,091; removed 2,025; brightened 5,161.

items.passage: Grant Packard and Jonah Berger analyzed the lyrics of approximately 4,200 songs that appeared on the Billboard charts and found that songs containing more second-person pronouns, such as “you,” tended to be more ______. In follow-up experiments, participants also liked such songs more and were more willing to purchase them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Successful means achieving popularity or good results. The second sentence confirms the point: in experiments, participants “liked such songs more and were more willing to purchase them,” so songs with more second-person pronouns tended to do better.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that songs using “you” more often stirred disagreement; the follow-up experiments show that participants liked them more and were more willing to buy them.

B.why_wrong: Forgettable means easily forgotten. The text says participants “liked such songs more and were more willing to purchase them,” which is hardly how a forgettable song would be received.

C.why_wrong: The text says listeners were more willing to buy such songs, not that the songs cost more.

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Packard and Berger 2020 (Psychological Science): textual analysis of songs ranked in the Billboard charts (N = 4,200) and experiments (N = 2,921) show that cultural items using more second-person pronouns are liked and purchased more

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology of culture). Key letter D. Restatement clue in the second sentence ('also liked such songs more'). Raw freq.txt ranks: controversial 33,131; forgettable unseen (a modern word the old corpus misses); expensive 6,205; successful 2,541. 'Repetitive' was dropped: songs with more 'you' repeat that word more, so it could be defended.

items.passage: English painter Marianne North (1830–1890) traveled to Brazil, Japan, India, Australia, Chile, and many other places to paint plants. Her oil paintings ______ plant life with scientific accuracy at a time before photography was a practical way to record it, and in 1882 a gallery displaying about 800 of them opened at Kew Gardens in London.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Documented means recorded in detail. The text says her paintings showed plant life “with scientific accuracy” at a time before photography was “a practical way to record it,” so the paintings served as a record of the plants she saw.

B.why_wrong: Invented means made up. Paintings made “with scientific accuracy” recorded real plants rather than imaginary ones.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that painting plants harmed them; North recorded plant life in her paintings.

D.why_wrong: The text says North traveled to paint plants, not to buy them, and paintings cannot purchase anything.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Marianne North (1830-1890): travels to Brazil, Japan, India, Australia, Chile and elsewhere; her paintings documented plant life with scientific accuracy before photography became a practical option; her gallery at Kew opened in 1882 with 800 oil paintings

items.notes: Subject: history (Victorian botany and art). Key letter A. Restatement clue: 'a practical way to record it'. Raw freq.txt ranks: documented 5,158; invented 6,273; harmed 1,345; purchased 4,388.

items.passage:
The following text is from Knut Hamsun’s 1917 novel Growth of the Soil (translated in 1920 by W. J. Alexander Worster). Isak and Inger are settlers building a farm in the Norwegian wilderness.

The weather <u>kept</u> fine, more or less. Inger got the potatoes in by herself, and Isak had the roofing done before the rain came on in earnest. The goats were brought in of a night into the hut and all slept there together; they managed somehow, they managed everyway, and did not grumble.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “kept” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used in the text, “kept” means remained. The weather stayed fine for a while, which let Inger get “the potatoes in” and Isak finish the roofing “before the rain came on in earnest.”

A.why_wrong: To keep can mean to save, as in keeping money, but weather cannot save anything; the text says the fine weather lasted.

C.why_wrong: To keep can mean to guard, as in keeping watch, but the sentence describes the weather staying fine, not protecting anything.

D.why_wrong: To keep can mean to restrain, as in keeping a dog back, but nothing in the sentence is being held back; the weather simply stayed fine.

items.passage:
The following text is from Charles G. D. Roberts’s 1902 short story “A Treason of Nature.” The story follows a bull moose inhabiting a forest beside a lake.

As a rule, the moose, for all his bulk and seeming clumsiness, moves through the forest as soundlessly as a weasel. He <u>plants</u> his wide hoofs like thistledown, insinuates his spread of antlers through the tangle like a snake, and befools his enemies with the nicest craft of the wilderness.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “plants” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used in the text, “plants” means places, or sets down. The moose “moves through the forest as soundlessly as a weasel,” so he sets each wide hoof down as lightly as thistledown.

A.why_wrong: To plant can mean to grow something by putting it in the soil, but the moose is not growing his hoofs; he is setting them down quietly.

B.why_wrong: To plant can mean to hide something where it will be found, but the text describes how the moose steps, not anything he conceals.

D.why_wrong: To plant can mean to establish, as in planting a colony, but that sense does not fit the moose’s footsteps.

items.notes: Subject: literature (animal story, 1902). Key letter C. Concrete physical sense of 'plant' (to set down firmly). Roberts appears in no official item and none of ours.

items.passage:
The following text is from W. H. Hudson’s 1904 novel Green Mansions. The narrator, a traveler in a South American forest, has been asked to settle a disagreement between Rima, a young woman, and her grandfather, Nuflo.

“Is it, then, left for me to decide?” said I, addressing the girl.

But though her face was towards me, she refused to meet my look and was silent. Silent, but not satisfied: she doubted still, and had perhaps <u>caught</u> something in my tone that strengthened her doubt.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “caught” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used in the text, “caught” means noticed. Rima “doubted still,” and something she heard “in my tone” made her doubt stronger, so she noticed something in the way the narrator spoke.

A.why_wrong: To catch can mean to grab with the hands, but a tone of voice cannot be grabbed; Rima notices something in it.

B.why_wrong: To catch can mean to contract an illness, but nothing in the text is about illness; the word describes what Rima heard.

C.why_wrong: To catch can mean to trap an animal, but the text describes Rima listening to the narrator, not trapping anything.

items.passage: Chou Wen-chung, a composer who emigrated from China to the United States in 1946, was profoundly ______ Chinese calligraphy, an art form he studied meticulously. In his 1963 composition Cursive, for example, he related the way ink flows from the brush in cursive script to the changing density of musical sound.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Inspired by means moved to create by. The text says Chou studied calligraphy “meticulously” and, in Cursive, “related the way ink flows from the brush in cursive script to the changing density of musical sound,” so calligraphy shaped his music.

B.why_wrong: Unaware of means not knowing about. Chou “studied meticulously” the calligraphy he drew on, so he was far from unaware of it.

C.why_wrong: Calligraphy is an art form, not an employer, and the text says nothing about Chou being hired to work in it.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests calligraphy frightened Chou; he studied it closely and used it as a model for his music.

items.passage: After turning from figurative painting to abstraction in the late 1940s, Turkish artist Fahrelnissa Zeid was evidently ______ working on an enormous scale: her monumental abstract canvases immerse viewers in kaleidoscopic patterns of color, and one of them, My Hell (1951), is approximately five meters wide.

items.passage: Like many other invasive ants, the clonal raider ant reproduces without mating and has multiple egg-laying females in each colony. Waring Trible and colleagues, who traced the species’ invasive populations to Bangladesh, suggest that such characteristics probably ______ its spread from there to other regions of the world, perhaps by way of historic shipping ports on the Bay of Bengal.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Aided means helped. The text says these characteristics are shared with “many other invasive ants,” species known for spreading into new places, so the characteristics probably helped the clonal raider ant spread beyond Bangladesh.

A.why_wrong: Prevented means stopped. The ant did spread from Bangladesh to other regions, and the traits it shares with other invasive ants would not have stopped that spread.

B.why_wrong: Traits such as reproducing without mating cannot record anything; the researchers, not the traits, traced the ant’s spread.

D.why_wrong: Traits do not predict events, and the text presents these characteristics as part of the reason the ant spread, not as a forecast of it.

items.passage: A 13-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a ground sloth discovered in Peru bears 46 tooth marks. Because the other crocodile relatives known from that region and period were either too small or had jaws suited to different kinds of feeding, François Pujos and Rodolfo Salas-Gismondi ______ that the marks were made by a young Purussaurus, a giant caiman.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Concluded means decided after reasoning. Because the other crocodile relatives in the region were “either too small or had jaws suited to different kinds of feeding,” the researchers ruled them out and reasoned that a young Purussaurus made the marks.

A.why_wrong: Doubted means questioned. The researchers ruled out the other crocodile relatives, which gave them a reason to accept, not doubt, that a young Purussaurus made the marks.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests the researchers were sorry about their finding; they reasoned their way to it.

C.why_wrong: Imagined suggests a guess with no evidence behind it, but the researchers based their view on evidence, ruling out the other crocodile relatives one by one.

items.passage: Chartered by Congress in 1865, the Freedman’s Savings Bank collected deposits from tens of thousands of Black Americans, many of them formerly enslaved. items.explanation: Withstand means to hold out against or survive. The text says that after the speculative loans and the financial panic, the bank “closed in 1874,” so it could not survive its losses.

A.why_wrong: The text does not discuss whether the bank hid its losses; it says the losses forced the bank to close.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that the bank could not work out how much it had lost; what it could not do was survive the losses.
